sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Leader election is the process by which a set of distributed nodes chooses exactly one node to act as the coordinator (primary, master, or leader) for some period; common algorithms include the **Bully algorithm** (highest-id wins), the **Ring algorithm** (token-passing on a logical ring), and **Raft-style voting** (majority-based with terms); production systems combine these with **leases** and **fencing tokens** to prevent split-brain.

Leader election solves a recurring problem in distributed systems: out of `N` identical nodes, exactly one must act as the coordinator — the writer, the scheduler, the sequencer, the gateway — to avoid the chaos of multiple nodes issuing conflicting decisions. The challenge is that nodes can crash, the network can partition, and clocks can drift, so the protocol must guarantee that at most one leader exists at any time (safety) and that a new leader is elected quickly when the old one fails (liveness). The classic algorithms — Bully, Ring, and the voting-based approach underlying Raft and Paxos — each make different trade-offs between message complexity, time complexity, and tolerance to failures. Real production systems rarely use the textbook algorithms directly; they layer on leases (a leader holds power for a bounded time, then must renew), fencing tokens (each leader gets a monotonically increasing epoch, and writes from older epochs are rejected), and witness nodes (a tie-breaker in even-sized clusters) to handle the edge cases the textbooks ignore.

The **Bully algorithm**, proposed by Garcia-Molina in 1982, is the simplest to reason about. Each node has a unique numeric id. When a node detects the leader has failed, it sends an election message to all nodes with higher ids. If any higher-id node responds, the original node steps aside; the higher-id node in turn sends its own election message. The node with the highest id that responds becomes the new leader and broadcasts a coordinator message. Its message complexity is O(N²) in the worst case, and it tolerates crash failures but not partitions — during a partition, two sides can each elect their own leader, causing split-brain. Bully is rarely used in production in its pure form, but its id-comparison principle appears in many systems (Kafka's controller election, MongoDB's replica set election, Redis Sentinel's master selection) as one input among many.

The **Ring algorithm** arranges nodes in a logical ring, each node knowing only its successor. When a node detects a failure, it sends an election message with its id to its successor; if the successor is down, it skips to the next. Each node appends its own id and forwards the message. When the message returns to the originator, it picks the highest id in the list and sends a coordinator message around the ring. The Ring algorithm has O(N²) message complexity worst-case but O(N) optimal if only the originating node forwards. Its advantage over Bully is that each node needs only to know its successor (O(1) membership state). Its disadvantage is the same as Bully's: no partition tolerance, and the elected leader may be the highest-id node even if it is not the best candidate (least loaded, most up-to-date).

**Raft-style voting** is the modern production standard. Each node has a term (logical clock), a voted-for record, and a log. When a follower does not hear from the leader within an election timeout, it increments the term, becomes a candidate, and requests votes from all other nodes. A node grants its vote if the candidate's term is higher than its own and the candidate's log is at least as up-to-date as its own (the up-to-date check ensures the new leader has all committed entries). The candidate wins if it receives a majority of votes for that term. The term mechanism prevents split-brain: at most one leader can be elected per term, because a node votes for at most one candidate per term, and a majority quorum cannot exist twice. Raft's voting is the basis of etcd, Consul, CockroachDB, and TiKV's leader election, and is widely adopted because it is formally proven safe and operationally simple.

Real-world systems extend these algorithms with **leases** to reduce the cost of failure detection. A lease is a time-bounded grant of leadership: the leader holds power for, say, 5 seconds, and must renew before expiry. If the leader crashes or partitions, the lease expires and a new leader can be elected without waiting for a heartbeat timeout. Leases require bounded clock drift (NTP, GPS) to be safe, because a lease expiry is a wall-clock event. Google's Chubby, Apache ZooKeeper, and Kubernetes' leader election all use leases. The **fencing token** (or epoch, term, generation number) is the second critical extension: every leader is associated with a monotonically increasing number, and every write carries it. Storage systems (HDFS, Kafka, GFS) reject writes with stale tokens, so even if a stale leader sends a write after the new leader has taken over, the storage rejects it.

The trade-off across all these algorithms is between failover speed and false positives. A short election timeout (e.g., 500ms) detects failures quickly but may trigger spurious elections during transient network blips, causing leader churn and reduced throughput. A long timeout (e.g., 30s) is stable but slow to recover from real failures. Production systems tune the timeout based on expected network characteristics (sub-millisecond within a rack, 1-2ms across AZ, 50-150ms cross-region) and use gradual timeouts: a fast initial heartbeat check followed by slower confirmation before declaring the leader dead. The architect's job is to understand that leader election is not a one-size-fits-all protocol but a family of mechanisms layered for safety (terms + fencing), liveness (heartbeats + leases), and performance (tunable timeouts) — and to choose the right combination for each workload's tolerance of unavailability and split-brain risk.

sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant N1 as Node 1 (id=1)
    participant N2 as Node 2 (id=2)
    participant N3 as Node 3 (id=3, leader)
    participant N4 as Node 4 (id=4)

    Note over N3: Current leader = Node 3
    N3--xN1: heartbeat (timeout)
    N3--xN2: heartbeat (timeout)
    Note over N3: Node 3 crashes
    N1->>N2: election(msg=1)
    N1->>N4: election(msg=1)
    N2->>N4: election(msg=1,2)
    N4-->>N2: OK (4>2)
    N4-->>N1: OK (4>1)
    Note over N4: Node 4 has highest id -> wins
    N4->>N1: coordinator(id=4, epoch=2)
    N4->>N2: coordinator(id=4, epoch=2)
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
            +--+    +--+    +--+    +--+
   ring  -> |1 | -> |2 | -> |3 | -> |4 | <- (3 is leader, crashes)
            +--+    +--+    +--+    +--+
                              X (down)

   N1 detects timeout, starts election (Bully style):
       N1 -> N2: "election, my id=1"
       N1 -> N4: "election, my id=1"
       N2 -> N4: "election, ids=[1,2]"
       N4 (highest): wins -> broadcasts "coordinator id=4, epoch=2"

   Fencing: every write carries epoch=2.
       old leader N3 (epoch=1) returns, sends write -> REJECTED (stale epoch)
```

### Walkthrough
1. The leader (Node 3) crashes. Nodes 1, 2, and 4 stop receiving heartbeats; their election timers fire.
2. Each node starts an election: Node 1 sends an election message to higher-id nodes (2 and 4); Node 2 sends to 4. Higher-id nodes respond, and the highest-id alive node (4) wins.
3. Node 4 broadcasts a coordinator message with a new epoch (2). All followers update their epoch. Any subsequent write from a stale leader (e.g., Node 3 if it recovers) carries epoch=1 and is rejected by the storage layer (fencing).

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
import random, time

class BullyNode:
    """Bully algorithm: highest-id alive node becomes leader."""
    def __init__(self, nid, all_nodes):
        self.id = nid
        self.all = all_nodes        # dict id -> node
        self.alive = True
        self.leader = None
        self.epoch = 0

    def start_election(self):
        if not self.alive:
            return None
        higher = [n for nid, n in self.all.items() if nid > self.id and n.alive]
        print(f"[N{self.id}] starts election, pings {len(higher)} higher nodes")
        # Bully: if any higher node responds, step aside
        responded = False
        for n in higher:
            if n.respond_to_election(self.id):
                responded = True
        if responded:
            return None              # wait for the higher node to become leader
        # No higher node responded -> I am the highest alive -> I am leader
        self.epoch += 1
        self.leader = self.id
        for n in self.all.values():
            if n.alive and n.id != self.id:
                n.ack_leader(self.id, self.epoch)
        print(f"[N{self.id}] is NEW LEADER (epoch={self.epoch})")
        return self.id

    def respond_to_election(self, caller_id):
        if not self.alive:
            return False
        if caller_id < self.id:
            print(f"  [N{self.id}] responds OK to N{caller_id} (will take over)")
            self.start_election()    # I will start my own election
            return True
        return False

    def ack_leader(self, leader_id, epoch):
        if epoch > self.epoch:
            self.epoch = epoch
            self.leader = leader_id
            print(f"  [N{self.id}] acks N{leader_id} as leader (epoch={epoch})")

# Build a 5-node Bully cluster
nodes = {i: BullyNode(i, {}) for i in range(1, 6)}
for n in nodes.values():
    n.all = nodes

# Initial leader = highest id alive
nodes[1].start_election()
print(f"  current leader: N{nodes[1].leader}\n")

# Simulate leader (id=5) crashing -> node 1 detects and starts election
nodes[5].alive = False
print("-- N5 crashes --")
nodes[1].start_election()
print(f"  current leader: N{nodes[1].leader}\n")

# Fencing: stale leader tries to write with old epoch
print("-- stale N5 'recovers', tries to write with old epoch=1 --")
nodes[5].alive = True
nodes[5].epoch = 1                   # stale epoch (real cluster is now at epoch=2)
print(f"  N5 sends write(epoch=1) -> STORAGE REJECTS (current epoch={nodes[1].epoch})")
```

quiz.explanation: In an even-sized cluster, a 50-50 partition splits the votes evenly, and neither side can reach a strict majority. With N=4 and a 2-2 split, no leader can be elected on either side, so the entire cluster becomes unavailable even though half the nodes are healthy on each side. This is strictly worse than an odd-sized cluster where one side always has the majority (e.g., N=3 with a 2-1 split, or N=5 with a 3-2 split).
